clue.text: Fanny makes only a fleeting final appearance in her act?

definitions.text: Fanny makes only a fleeting final appearance in her act?

blocks.clueFragment: Fanny makes only a fleeting final appearance
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman named Fanny who turns up only briefly at the end
setter's reading: fanny is British slang for the genitals, glimpsed only at the climax of a certain kind of performance

explanation.walkthrough: Fanny reads as a name, but in British slang it is a vulgar word for the female genitals; the act in question ends with everything coming off.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who undresses for an audience reveals the most only at the very end of the routine.

clue.text: (& 21ac.) Don't speak of supports applied to hot belly

blocks.note: to support them financially
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
tum is a nursery word for the stomach

explanation.surface: Advice not to mention the props someone has strapped to a warm paunch.
explanation.walkthrough: SHTUM is British slang, from Yiddish, for silent; to keep shtum about something is to say nothing of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay silent about a matter is to refuse to talk of it, so the phrase is an idiom for discretion.

clue.text: (see 10ac.)
Observer's irritated by this middling piece from busty Eve

indicators.note: a piece taken from the middle of the following words means the letters sit inside them

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A spectator is bothered by a glimpse of a well-endowed woman called Eve.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer here is not the newspaper but the eye, the organ that observes.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflamed swelling on the eyelid is something that irritates the organ of sight.

clue.text: Rapidly depressing key activity — a bit like a Tory rag?

blocks.note: the Daily Telegraph is a British newspaper that backs the Conservatives
the suffix -y turns a noun into 'like that thing', as in leathery

explanation.surface: Sounds like a gloomy activity, compared with reading a right-wing newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Depressing means pressing down, not saddening: the operator taps a Morse key quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Sending messages by wire meant pressing a Morse key up and down at speed, the very activity described.

clue.text: Well, Brenda's a rubbish TV host

blocks.note: a spring is a natural well of water
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER; the 's is the attaching apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that Brenda is a hopeless presenter.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerry Springer hosted a notoriously trashy US talk show. Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerry Springer fronted a confrontational chat show widely derided as trash television.

clue.text: Sir's top removed by gay — reassuring for those who go fearfully to bed?

definitions.text: reassuring for those who go fearfully to bed?

indicators.note: taking off the top of a word in a down clue drops its first letter

blocks.note: a man addressed as Sir has been knighted
gay in its old sense of carefree, light-hearted

explanation.surface: A knight loses his head to a gay man, which somehow comforts nervous sleepers.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K of KNIGHT is the top to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A dim lamp left on overnight soothes children or adults who are scared of the dark.

clue.text: "Go down sportingly" tip from Prescott, just a hoax

indicators.note: the tip of a name in a down clue is its extremity, here the closing letter

blocks.note: to ski is to go down a slope as a sport
John Prescott was Blair's Deputy Prime Minister

explanation.surface: John Prescott advises losing gracefully, and it turns out to be a wind-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A short satirical sketch is a send-up, a piece of mockery rather than anything serious.

clue.text: Blair's political position as determined by focus groups?

definitions.text: Blair's political position as determined by focus groups?

blocks.note: surface reading: where New Labour stood on the left-right spectrum
setter's reading: a focus is a central point, so groups of focuses would fix the middle ground

explanation.walkthrough: Blair's New Labour was accused of setting policy by focus groups; the joke is that a focus is literally a central point.
explanation.definitionFit: Blair placed New Labour in the political middle ground between traditional left and right.

clue.text: (& 3dn.) By whom a man gets hardened to the frustration of non-consummation

definitions.text: By whom a man gets hardened to the frustration of non-consummation

blocks.clueFragment: a man gets hardened to the frustration
blocks.note: surface reading: someone grows used to disappointment
setter's reading: hardened is literal, a man aroused by someone who never follows through

explanation.walkthrough: Hardened looks like 'grown inured'; it is meant physically. Prick is vulgar slang for the penis.
explanation.definitionFit: The vulgar term names someone who arouses a man sexually with no intention of going any further.

clue.text: Cyclops has had his day in a blind alley

blocks.note: the setter, speaking as himself, says I'm
passé means out of date, past its best

explanation.surface: The setter, washed up, finds himself stuck at a dead end.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter, so the statement 'Cyclops has had his day' becomes, in his own voice, I'M PASSÉ.
explanation.definitionFit: An impasse is a dead end, a street with no way through, as well as a deadlock.

clue.text: Apt description of end of willie (mine) with article stuck in it

indicators.note: something stuck in a word is pushed inside it, so one piece goes within another
'end of' keeps only the last letter of 'willie'

blocks.note: the closing letter of willie
a pit is a coal mine
the definite article

explanation.surface: The setter boasts that a certain word suits the tip of his own member, which has something lodged in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Mine looks possessive, the setter's own willie; it is a noun, a pit. Willie is British slang for the penis.
explanation.definitionFit: An epithet is a descriptive word or phrase attached to a name, ideally a fitting one.

clue.text: (& 15ac.) Blair-Brown thing that could bring about a split? Might to Labour

definitions.text: Blair-Brown thing that could bring about a split?

blocks.note: might is strength
to labour is to toil with difficulty

explanation.surface: The Blair-Brown rivalry could split the party, so strength to the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour looks like the political party, which suits Blair and Brown; here it is the verb for hard toil.
explanation.definitionFit: Blair and Brown's long rivalry for the Labour leadership was a contest for control that threatened to divide the party.

clue.text: Ex-president's not getting an erection after cleaning up act

indicators.note: in a down clue an erection raises a word, so it reads from the bottom upward

blocks.note: washing is the act of cleaning
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former president is impotent after a scandal-cleansing exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Ex-president is 'is'; the reversed word follows the washing.
explanation.definitionFit: George Washington was the first President of the United States.

clue.text: (see 13ac.)
Figures some Tory leaders are implicated in something shocking to a point

indicators.note: to be implicated in something is to be caught up inside it

blocks.note: static electricity gives a small shock
T's, the Tory leaders, written as T IS
south, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Data show some Conservative bosses mixed up in a scandal, up to a point.
explanation.walkthrough: Static electricity is what gives the small jolt; the point is one of the four compass points, added last.
explanation.definitionFit: Statistics are numerical data, the figures collected and analysed.

clue.text: Jagger finally set to change — a museum piece now, this Stone

definitions.text: a museum piece now, this Stone

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the name it follows
letters told to change are rearranged into a new order

blocks.note: Mick Jagger, singer of the Rolling Stones
taken as written
taken as written; it looks like a link word but is fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mick Jagger is now a museum relic, this aging Rolling Stone.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is 'set to', both words; the 'to' is easily mistaken for a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rosetta Stone, key to deciphering hieroglyphs, is displayed in the British Museum.

clue.text: Pitiful groping?

blocks.note: first meaning: moving, arousing pity
second meaning: feeling with the hands

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like a sneer at a clumsy pass; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both emotionally affecting and making physical contact with the hands.

clue.text: Soldier who's dropped dog's butt on model

indicators.note: a butt is the tail end of something, so only its closing letter is kept

blocks.note: a paratrooper is dropped by parachute
the closing letter of dog
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier drops a cigarette end from a dog-end onto a fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropped looks like 'let fall'; it describes how a paratrooper arrives. A dog-end is British slang for a cigarette butt.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a perfect example to be copied, a model of excellence.

clue.text: Tone: "Am in trouble — put somebody up for election"

indicators.note: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder and come out rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it doubles as part of the signal

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, called Tone, admits he is in difficulty and backs a candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: Tone is a familiar form of Tony Blair's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To nominate is to propose someone formally as a candidate in a vote.

clue.text: Girl star having sex by yard — it leads to rupture

blocks.note: Di is a short girl's name
the sun is a star
it is slang for sex
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A starlet having sex in a yard risks an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupture suggests a hernia; it means a break between people.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of agreement within a group is what leads to a split or breach.

clue.text: (see 2dn.)
Undercover items? The last things we'd print

blocks.note: first meaning: underwear, worn under the outer clothes
second meaning: small ads, which close the magazine

explanation.walkthrough: Undercover suggests spies; it means worn beneath clothing. Smalls is British slang for underwear, and also for classified small ads, which Private Eye prints at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both underclothes and classified small advertisements, the final pages of the magazine.

clue.text: VIP celebrity robber not good and randy

indicators.note: not good means without a letter standing for good, which must be taken out

blocks.note: Ronnie Biggs, the notorious Great Train Robber
hot means sexually aroused

explanation.surface: A famous criminal VIP who is lustful and no good.
explanation.walkthrough: G is the standard abbreviation for good, removed from BIGGS. Randy is British slang for lustful.
explanation.definitionFit: A big shot is an important, influential person, a very important person.

clue.text: It's good to wallow in flipping blubber, gentlemen …!

indicators.note: flipping a word turns it over so its letters run the other way
something wallowing in a substance is surrounded by it

blocks.note: to blubber is to sob
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: An exclamation that wallowing in whale fat is a fine thing for the chaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Gentlemen is the gents, a men's lavatory; bogs is British slang for toilets.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gentlemen is a sign for a men's toilet, and bogs is slang for lavatories.

clue.text: Mock serious stiff one when embracing Penny

indicators.note: pieces embracing something hold it between them

blocks.note: a stiff is a corpse
an is the indefinite article, meaning one
P is the abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: A sarcastic remark about an erection that grips a woman named Penny.
explanation.walkthrough: Stiff one suggests the surface's erection; stiff is a corpse and one is the article, and the two clasp the coin between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan delivery feigns gravity with an expressionless face, a mock-serious manner.

clue.text: … like a pig stuck up prima donna

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending a word up makes it read from the bottom

blocks.note: greedy as a pig, avid

explanation.surface: Continuing from the clue above, a conceited opera star is piggish.
explanation.walkthrough: Stuck up looks like 'conceited', describing the diva; it is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A prima donna is the leading female singer in an opera, also called a diva.

clue.text: Killjoy Prince dominating Diana endlessly

indicators.note: without its end, a name loses its closing letter
in a down clue, dominating means sitting above, so that letter comes first

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for prince
Diana Rigg, actress famous from The Avengers

explanation.surface: A spoilsport prince bullies Diana without end, evoking Charles and Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: Diana suggests the Princess of Wales, but here it is the actress Diana Rigg.
explanation.definitionFit: A prig is a self-righteous, censorious person who spoils others' fun.

clue.text: Member's area: enter to accept Blair's end

indicators.note: the end of a name is its closing letter
accepting something takes it inside

blocks.note: to enter is to go in
the closing letter of Blair

explanation.surface: An MP's constituency is told to admit the Prime Minister's final act.
explanation.walkthrough: Member looks like a Member of Parliament; it is the penis.
explanation.definitionFit: The groin is the region where the legs meet the body, where the male member is found.

clue.text: Agreeable schedule that keeps Brenda and co. going

definitions.text: schedule that keeps Brenda and co. going

blocks.note: civil means polite, courteous
a schedule is a list

explanation.surface: A pleasant timetable that keeps the royal family busy.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen; the Civil List was the annual sum Parliament paid to fund the royal household.
explanation.definitionFit: The Civil List was the state payment funding the monarch and family, keeping the royals in money.
